sources.citation: Voegelin, C.F. & F.M. Voegelin. 1964. Languages of the World: African Fascicle One. Anthropological Linguistics 6(5). (ERIC microfiche scan, archive.org micro_IA41153350_0260)
sources.note: Talodi branch section 1.7.3 is purely classificatory ('Moro Hills.. Part of Acheron village'); the 'stress unit' passage surfaced by full-text search is about Berber. Irrelevant.

sources.citation: Spronk, Tanya. 2004. A brief description of the current Talodi orthographies. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 119-126. SIL-Sudan.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a catalogue record only (no print holding to request from, no digital copy known)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Sec. 5.5 Tone: 'Norton (1994) reports that there is no contrastive tone in Asharon, while Jacob (1996) has reported some minimal pairs for High and Low tone in Tocco.' Cites Norton 1994 'Phonology and Orthography Issues in Asharon', unpublished ms.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell J. 2021. Participatory word spacing in Acheron preverbal inflection. SIL Electronic Working Papers 132. Dallas: SIL International. iii+10 pp. (SIL archives item 89096, via the Internet Archive)
sources.note: No Acheron stress statement. Lists generic wordhood criterion 'phonological unity (words are domains for prosodic processes of stress, tone, or vowel harmony)' (p.3) but applies only pause/elision/separability tests; fn.5 p.7: 'Tone marks are absent because tones (as opposed to intonational phrases) are extremely rare in this language (Norton 2013:205).'

sources.citation: Quint, Nicolas. 2020. Kordofanian. In R. Vossen & G. Dimmendaal (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of African Languages. OUP. (HAL halshs-03093501)
sources.note: Family-level only: 'probably all Kordofanian languages are tone languages (with generally two tone levels..)'. Nothing specific to Acheron; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Smits, Heleen. 2017. A grammar of Lumun, a Kordofanian language of Sudan. Vol. 1. Utrecht: LOT (LOT 465).
sources.note: Describes sister language Lumun [lmd] as tonal (ch. 3 Tone); mentions Acheron only for classification, lexicostatistics and noun-class parallels (Norton 2000, 2013). Nothing on Acheron stress.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell & Thomas Kuku Alaki. 2015. The Talodi languages: a comparative-historical analysis. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 11: 31-161. SIL.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a catalogue record only (no print holding to request from, no digital copy known)
sources.note: Sec. 3.2.5 'Note on Length and Tone' (p.107): 'We omit analysis of prosodic features for lack of data and for lack of functional load.. There are no good vowel length contrasts in Talodi languages.. phonetically long vowels occur in non-final environments or monosyllabic words (Schadeberg 1981, Norton 1995, Alaki & Norton 2013).. Sources repeatedly show two tone levels in Talodi languages.. but tone is often contextually determined and minimal pairs are rare.' No stress statement for Acheron or the family.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell. 2013. The Acheron vowel system: a participatory approach. In Thilo C. Schadeberg & Roger M. Blench (eds.), Nuba Mountain Language Studies, 195-217. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe. (author PDF in SIL Language & Culture Archives item 67418, via the Internet Archive)
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent anywhere (0 hits for stress, accent, prominence, rhythm, penult). Only prosodic remark, p.205: 'Tone has a low lexical load in Acheron: no tonal contrasts were reported in Norton (1995), and of 336 monosyllabic and disyllabic words.. we identified just one word pair where contrast was due to tone'; high tone associates with /ə/.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell J. 2000. The noun classes of Asheron. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 8: 23-55. SIL-Sudan.
sources.note: Only a segment inventory (sec. 0.1, p.24) plus: 'Tone marks are absent.. tones are not exhibited by Asheron nouns in general.' Refers to Norton (1995) for phonology. Nothing on stress (the stress passages elsewhere in OPSL 8 are Gilley on Shilluk).

sources.citation: Alamin Mubarak, Suzan. 2012. An Initial Syntactic Analysis of Asheron (A Nuba Mountain Language). Saarbrücken: LAP Lambert Academic Publishing, 104 pp. (rev. of 2002/2003 University of Khartoum M.A. thesis).

sources.note: Only other book-length description; Khartoum theses usually open with a phonology overview that may state stress/tone status.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell. 1994. Phonology and Orthography Issues in Asharon. Unpublished manuscript, SIL-Sudan, Khartoum (cited in Spronk 2004, OPSL 9).

sources.note: Phonology-and-orthography statement underlying the Acheron orthography; orthography statements of this kind normally say whether stress/tone is contrastive and where prominence falls.

sources.access_detail: held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number PL8571.N83 2013); the library holds the journal volume but the item itself was not found; ask your own library for a scan or interlibrary loan
sources.note: Tocho [taz] is Acheron's closest relative (72% lexical similarity, same 8-vowel system, partial mutual intelligibility); a full phonology sketch by the same author may contain an explicit stress statement transferable as family context (not a substitute for Acheron).

sources.note: The only full phonological description of Acheron (both E and W dialects); repeatedly cited by Norton 2000/2013/2015 for tone, vowel length and sound change, so it is the one place a stress/accent statement would be. Would supersede everything found.
